name: Canadian CT Head Rule

citations.text: Stiell IG, Wells GA, Vandemheen K, et al. The Canadian CT Head Rule for patients with minor head injury. Lancet. 2001;357(9266):1391-1396.

validated_population: Adults 16 and older with a minor head injury (passed out, memory loss, or confusion afterward) who were alert on arrival (GCS 13 to 15). People taking blood thinners were excluded.
self_report_note: The rule was validated with a clinician assessing alertness (Glasgow Coma Scale). Someone who was not injured should answer for the injured person when possible.
license_note: Published clinical decision rule; criteria are not a copyrighted instrument. Question wording is original to OLA BOT.

red_flags.question: Has the person had a seizure, or are they getting more drowsy or harder to wake?
red_flags.help: Answer yes for any shaking episode, or if the person is becoming sleepier.

red_flags.question: Is there weakness or numbness on one side of the body, or are the pupils different sizes?
red_flags.help: Look at both pupils (black centers of the eyes) in normal light.

items.question: How old is the injured person?
items.help: The rule was validated for people 16 and older.

items.question: Does the person take a blood thinner? (For example warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or clopidogrel.)
items.help: Blood thinners raise the risk of bleeding in the brain. Daily low-dose aspirin alone is a no.

items.question: After the injury, did the person pass out, lose memory of the event, or seem confused or disoriented?
items.help: Answer yes for any passing out, any gap in memory about the injury, or any confusion seen by others.
items.trace_label: Passed out, memory loss, or confusion (rule applies)

items.question: Two hours or more after the injury, is the person still not fully alert or not answering questions normally?
items.help: Ask the person their name, where they are, and today's date.
items.trace_label: High risk: not fully alert 2 hours after injury (GCS <15)

items.question: Is there a dent in the skull, or an open wound where the skull might be broken?
items.help: Feel gently around the injury. Do not press into an open wound.
items.trace_label: High risk: possible open or depressed skull fracture

items.question: Is there bruising around both eyes or behind an ear, or clear fluid or blood coming from the nose or ears?
items.help: These are signs of a break at the base of the skull.
items.trace_label: High risk: signs of basal skull fracture

items.question: Has the person vomited 2 or more times since the injury?
items.help: Count separate episodes of throwing up.
items.trace_label: High risk: vomiting 2 or more times

items.question: Is there memory loss for 30 minutes or more of the time BEFORE the injury?
items.help: Ask the person what they were doing in the half hour before the injury.
items.trace_label: Medium risk: memory loss ≥30 minutes before injury

items.question: Was it a dangerous injury? (Hit by a vehicle as a pedestrian, thrown from a vehicle, or a fall from more than 3 feet or 5 stairs.)
items.help: Answer yes if any of these happened.

scoring.threshold_text: Applies only after passing out, memory loss, or confusion. High risk (any): not alert at 2 hours, skull fracture signs, vomiting ≥2, age 65+. Medium risk (any): memory loss ≥30 min before injury, dangerous mechanism. Otherwise low risk (CT not required).

steps.label: No passing out, memory loss, or confusion (rule does not apply)

overrides.label: Takes a blood thinner (excluded from the rule)

high.label: High risk: head CT recommended
high.interpretation: A high-risk factor is present. The rule recommends a CT scan of the head to check for an injury that may need surgery.
high.recommendation: Go to an emergency department now for evaluation and a head CT.

care.where_detail: Hospital emergency department with CT scanning. Do not drive yourself.
ed_redirect: Seizure, worsening drowsiness, or repeated vomiting: call 911
Weakness on one side or unequal pupils: call 911

medium.label: Medium risk: head CT advised
medium.interpretation: A medium-risk factor is present. The rule advises a CT scan to look for brain injury.
medium.recommendation: Go to an emergency department today for evaluation and a possible head CT.

care.where_detail: Hospital emergency department with CT scanning. Do not drive yourself.
ed_redirect: Seizure, worsening drowsiness, or repeated vomiting: call 911
Worst headache, weakness, or trouble speaking: call 911

low.label: Low risk: head CT not required
low.interpretation: No high- or medium-risk factors are present. By the Canadian CT Head Rule, a CT scan is not required. A concussion is still possible.
low.recommendation: Rest at home with another adult present for the next 24 hours. Get checked if symptoms persist.

care.within: Home observation for 24 hours; primary care within 2 to 3 days if symptoms persist
care.where_detail: Home care with another adult present. Book a primary care visit if headache, dizziness, or trouble concentrating continue.
self_care: Have another adult stay with you for 24 hours.
Rest your brain and body; avoid alcohol and driving.

no_criteria.label: Minor head bump (rule does not apply)
no_criteria.interpretation: There was no passing out, memory loss, or confusion. The CT Head Rule applies only when one of these happened. A head bump without them is usually minor.
no_criteria.recommendation: Watch for warning signs at home for the next 24 hours.

care.where_detail: Home care. Book a primary care visit if headache or other symptoms last more than a few days.

anticoagulated.label: Blood thinner: needs evaluation
anticoagulated.interpretation: People taking blood thinners were excluded from the Canadian CT Head Rule. Head injuries on blood thinners carry a higher risk of bleeding in the brain, and a CT scan is usually advised.
anticoagulated.recommendation: Go to an emergency department for evaluation. Bring your medication list.

care.where_detail: Hospital emergency department with CT scanning.

child.label: Rule does not apply (under 16)
child.interpretation: The Canadian CT Head Rule was not validated in children. Children with head injuries are assessed with different rules (such as PECARN) by a clinician.
child.recommendation: Have a clinician examine the child today.

care.where_detail: Pediatric urgent care or a hospital emergency department that treats children.
ed_redirect: Passed out, vomiting, or not acting normally: go to the emergency department
Seizure or very hard to wake: call 911
